title: Melbourne Firebombing Destroys Indian Couple's Dream Cafe Built With Their Life Savings
excerpt: Ashish Sharma and Manali Purohit opened their vegan cafe And Bodega in Fitzroy North in July. Three months later, an arson attack on the tobacco shop next door left it a burnt-out shell.
body:
• Ashish Sharma and Manali Purohit's Melbourne vegan cafe, And Bodega, was destroyed on October 12 when a firebombing targeted the tobacco shop next door, three months after the cafe opened.
  • The couple had put more than $100,000 of their life savings and five months of DIY work into the business; about $5,000 worth of equipment was stolen from the burnt-out premises the following day.
  • Victoria Police believe at least one offender forced entry into the tobacconist and set it alight. No arrests have been made, and police say there is nothing to suggest the targeted shop was selling illicit tobacco.
  • The attack is one of more than 150 firebombings of tobacconists in Victoria since March 2023, and the couple has joined calls for Australia to cut its tobacco excise to shrink the illegal cigarette market driving the violence.

Ashish Sharma and Manali Purohit spent five months fitting out their dream cafe themselves, scouring Facebook Marketplace for second-hand furniture, painting walls and installing plumbing. Their vegan cafe, And Bodega, opened on St Georges Road in Melbourne's Fitzroy North in July. In the early hours of Monday, October 12, it was destroyed by a fire that was not aimed at them at all.

Emergency services were called at about 3.45am after locals reported explosions at the tobacco shop that had recently opened next door. Investigators believe at least one offender forced entry into the tobacconist and deliberately set it alight, according to Victoria Police reporting carried by AAP. The blaze destroyed the tobacco shop, devastated And Bodega and damaged another cafe on the strip. No injuries were reported.

"It felt like a warzone. The roof had melted off — soot everywhere."

— Ashish Sharma, co-owner, And Bodega

A second blow the next day

The fire was not the end of it. The day after the firebombing, about $5,000 worth of technology and equipment was stolen from the burnt-out cafe. When the couple walked back into the premises after the robbery, Sharma said it felt as though their "dream had been ripped away." Small canisters from the explosions were strewn across the cafe floor.

Purohit, who grew up in Mumbai and trained as a pastry chef in India, had built the cafe's plant-based menu around her baking. The name And Bodega was a nod to the neighbourhood convenience stores of New York. The couple, who are newlyweds, had sunk more than $100,000 into the business. "We put in basically all our life savings. We did a lot of it DIY," Sharma told The Guardian.

Warnings before the fire

The couple say the risk was visible before the attack. They had initially welcomed the new neighbour, believing it would be a grocery store. When it became clear the shop might instead sell tobacco, customers began voicing fears of an arson attack. In late September, Purohit arrived for an early baking shift to find smashed glass at the neighbouring shop and a handwritten note on its wall, attributed by a witness who spoke to AAP to a group known as The Commission. Last Thursday, the shopfront glass was smashed again, with CCTV allegedly capturing bricks being hurled from a passing car.

Their cafe is collateral damage in what police and retailers describe as Victoria's tobacco wars: more than 150 tobacconist stores across the state have been targeted since March 2023, AAP reported, with hundreds hit across Melbourne since late 2023.

A tax fight behind the fires

Facing a damage bill of well over $100,000, Sharma has joined industry experts and economists calling for Australia's tobacco excise to be cut so that cheap illegal cigarettes lose their market. The Australian Bureau of Statistics estimates about 80 per cent of tobacco consumed in 2025 was illegal, up from 12 per cent in 2017, while the excise has more than tripled and raised $7.4 billion in 2024-25. The federal government is holding to a law-enforcement approach; the opposition coalition has vowed to cut the excise by 80 per cent if elected. Experts are split: Deakin University criminologist James Martin argues only a price cut addresses demand, while University of Sydney professor Becky Freeman warns a cut risks a "race to the bottom with criminals" and higher smoking rates.

What happens next

The couple have set up a crowdfunding campaign to pay for repairs and replacement equipment, outstanding staff and supplier costs, and a new home for And Bodega. Fellow small businesses have offered to donate portions of their profits, host fundraisers and drop off ice-cream. "The only reason we're positive is because of the people," Sharma said. "It's really overwhelming the love and support." Police are examining CCTV from the area and have appealed for dashcam or security footage; anyone with information can contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.
